sentences.text: At Sveti Duh there is a ledge on the north wall of the church, about two metres up, where the buttress meets the stone, and it is about the size of a windowsill and it is where you put things out.
You put out four or five objects.
Never one; one is not a trade, it is an offering, and an offering gets left exactly where you put it.
You put them out at dusk and you go away.

Going away is not optional and it is not superstition; anybody who has ever waited round that corner has got nothing, and the village's explanation for this is that she can hear you, which is almost certainly correct.
Nobody watches.
There is no tradition of watching and there is no story in Sveti Duh about anybody having seen the exchange, and Jakob has never met a person who claimed to.
In the morning one of them is gone and there is something else in its place, and the something else is always better.
Not more valuable.

Nobody in that village has ever got a coin off that ledge and Jakob's grandmother would tell you, at some length, about a man in the 1960s who put out a watch and a ring and two buttons in an attempt to establish an exchange rate, and who got back a piece of blue glass, and who was extremely annoyed about it for eleven years and who kept the glass until he died.
Better means better.
That is the whole of the definition and there is not a better one available, and everybody in Sveti Duh finds this obvious and no visitor ever has.
What comes off that ledge, in Jakob's lifetime: a bootlace.
A key.
A plastic dinosaur.
Four marbles that he knows of.
A brass washer.
A cigarette lighter that did not work.
A piece of dark green sea glass from a coast three hundred kilometres away that caused a certain amount of discussion in 2014.
There is no pattern in the objects.
The pattern, if there is one, is entirely in who got which, and it is not a pattern you can see from outside a family.
The marten is a pine marten and she lives in the roof of the barn behind the church and she has been seen perhaps thirty times in Jakob's life, mostly as a shape going along a wall at speed.
She is not tame and she is not friendly and she has bitten one person, in 1998, who reached up onto the ledge while she was on it, which everybody agreed at the time was entirely his own fault.
Martens take shiny things.
That is well documented and every naturalist Jakob has ever mentioned it to has said so within about a minute.
They are curious, they cache, they will carry off a spoon, and there are people all over central Europe who have lost car keys to one.
The village has never disputed a word of that.
The village's position, as Jakob's grandmother put it, is that knowing what an animal does is not the same as knowing what it is doing.
